field_rule: Hooded windmillgrass generally has crowded shorter racemes (~2–5 cm) and a conspicuous rounded sterile hood with short awns. Tumble windmillgrass typically has longer (~5–15 cm) racemes in separated tiers and longer awns. Feather fingergrass commonly has a feathery terminal fan with long apical fertile-lemma hairs. The hybrid may be intermediate.
trait_provenance: Existing Hays Botany Poaceae species card morphology; preliminary multi-access character states; needs field QA

head.source: Kew GrassBase; Texas Hill Country 2015; Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas
head.reference: 10–20 short (2–5 cm) racemes close together at apex; treatments describe one whorl or 1–3 closely spaced whorls. Broad visual coding allows both digitate and whorled; do not equate with C. verticillata's well-separated tiers.

ligule.source: Diggs et al. Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, 1999, user-provided monocots PDF
ligule.reference: p.180 (printed 1256): one terminal whorl of short 2–5cm branches, not several spaced tiers; ciliate membranous ligule

diagnostic_checks.look: Isolate the upper sterile floret
diagnostic_checks.check: Its upper sterile lemma is expanded into a markedly rounded, inflated, hood-like body approximately 1–1.5 mm long. This is a real sterile floral part, not swollen seed tissue.
diagnostic_checks.compare: tumble windmillgrass's upper sterile lemma is more oblong, often carrying a longer awn
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Kew GrassBase-backed; photo dissection pending
diagnostic_checks.source: Kew POWO / GrassBase — Chloris cucullata

diagnostic_checks.look: Compare both kinds of awn
diagnostic_checks.check: Published lower fertile-lemma awn around 0.3–1.5 mm and the upper sterile-lemma awn to about 1.5 mm: far shorter than tumble windmillgrass's several-mm awns.
diagnostic_checks.compare: C. verticillata; the hybrid can overlap and should not be diagnosed from one awn
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Kew GrassBase-backed; photo dissection pending
diagnostic_checks.source: Kew POWO / GrassBase — Chloris cucullata

diagnostic_checks.look: Inspect how tightly the short rays cluster
diagnostic_checks.check: Often 10–20 racemes of about 2–5 cm close together in 1–3 very tight apical whorls. Older keys may say 'one whorl'; do not exclude a hooded specimen merely for a few adjacent tiers.
diagnostic_checks.compare: C. verticillata's widely separated, longer tiered racemes
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Different floras describe 1 vs closely spaced whorls; broad key must tolerate both
diagnostic_checks.source: Kew GrassBase + Texas Hill Country regional descriptions

diagnostic_review.note: Measurements are published source descriptions, not verified dimensions on local photographed specimens; do not certify a field ID using head outline alone.

field_rule: Panicles often overlap. Show spring/autumn phase, true leaf collar, and at least three mature measured spikelets from the same plant before a firm species call.
trait_provenance: Existing Hays Botany Poaceae species card morphology; preliminary multi-access character states; needs field QA

head.reference: Open relatively few-flowered panicle ~5–10 cm with wiry stems; seasonal phase and look-alikes require photo examination.

ligule.source: FNA Dichanthelium commutatum (ciliate membrane ~0.3 mm) versus WFO short hair fringe or absent
ligule.reference: A tiny true membrane topped by longer cilia may appear like hairs or be completely worn/indiscernible; accept hairlike, membrane and absent-looking broad visual choices. Absence of visible ligule in a photo is not true anatomical absence.

diagnostic_checks.look: Check spring versus summer–fall flowering heads on ONE identified plant
diagnostic_checks.check: Flora of North America reports primary OPEN spring panicles about 5–12 cm, often April–June, and secondary mostly self-fertilizing (cleistogamous) small panicles from June to fall. Fall branches with reduced leaves may carry heads partly hidden by the flag sheaths.
diagnostic_checks.compare: D. oligosanthes also makes fall reduced panicles; seasonal head alone proves the genus, not the species.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: FNA spring/autumn account; no time-series same-plant local photos certified
diagnostic_checks.source: Flora of North America — Dichanthelium commutatum

diagnostic_checks.look: Open the short ligule and inspect the leaf-base attachment
diagnostic_checks.check: FNA describes an approximately 0.3 mm CILIATE MEMBRANE, with cilia longer than the membrane and occasionally long neighboring hairs. Leaves can have asymmetrical, cordate-clasping bases with 9–13 prominent veins.
diagnostic_checks.compare: D. oligosanthes commonly has a conspicuous band of hairs ~1–3 mm with narrower blades; D. pedicellatum has very narrow leaves and a cormlike base.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: FNA vs WFO which may call the minute ligule a fringe or absent: preserve all three FIELD-APPEARANCE options; actual tissue needs magnification
diagnostic_checks.source: FNA Dichanthelium commutatum (compare World Flora Online)

diagnostic_checks.look: Measure the two-floret spikelet and glume proportions
diagnostic_checks.check: Typical FNA spring spikelets about 2.2–3.2 mm long, pubescent, with a short LOWER glume ~0.7–1.8 mm and upper glume plus sterile lower lemma near spikelet length; hardened fertile upper floret has an often tiny raised apex.
diagnostic_checks.compare: D. oligosanthes spikelets overlap but are generally broader/rounder and 2.7–4.2 mm; check both against ruler and upper-glume vein prominence.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Species/taxon variety variability; same-plant dissected glumes and fertility unconfirmed
diagnostic_checks.source: Flora of North America — Dichanthelium commutatum

diagnostic_review.note: Source-backed flowering phase/ligule/spikelet checklists; no same-plant spring/fall/winter photo certification or confirmed Hays County voucher.

ligule.source: Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, monocots excerpt p.224 under Panicum oligosanthes; existing Hays species card
ligule.reference: Flora reports ligule length 0.1–4.2 mm varying between varieties, while Hays card reports hair fringe. Do not treat length or a distant collar photo as a species-level separator.

winter_rosette.source: FNA D. oligosanthes; Texas A&M Scribner Dichanthelium (variety example)
winter_rosette.reference: Well-developed basal winter rosette, primary spring and secondary summer-fall flowering panicles. The Texas variety illustration is NOT automatically exact species/variety confirmation for gallery records.

diagnostic_checks.look: Locate the genuine WINTER rosette and spring flowering culm
diagnostic_checks.check: FNA describes a well-differentiated basal winter rosette of several ovate/lanceolate blades ~2–6 cm, then stiffly erect vernal culms ~20–75 cm. Later stems can branch into bushy little fascicles with reduced blades.
diagnostic_checks.compare: D. pedicellatum is specifically documented as NOT rosette-forming and instead has a tiny shallow cormlike base. Do not require a winter rosette for every Dichanthelium.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: FNA and Texas A&M genus/variety examples; actual November–February rooted rosette remains photo-pending
diagnostic_checks.source: Flora of North America — Dichanthelium oligosanthes

diagnostic_checks.look: Compare spring open and late short PANICLES, not separate species
diagnostic_checks.check: Primary spring panicles about 5–9 cm with ~6–60 spikelets; later secondary panicles can be short, included in sheaths and self-fertilizing. A winter rosette with no visible head is a vegetative candidate, NOT a finished species call.
diagnostic_checks.compare: D. commutatum also produces spring open heads and later concealed selfing heads, so measure spikelets and leaf morphology.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: FNA seasonal phase account; individual fall head photo not checked
diagnostic_checks.source: Flora of North America — Dichanthelium oligosanthes

diagnostic_checks.look: Magnify the orange/purple upper-glume base and true hair ligule
diagnostic_checks.check: Spikelets ~2.7–4.2 mm, often broadened/obovoid, with a strongly veined UPPER glume sometimes orange-to-purple at the base; true ligule 1–3 mm of hairs. In some Texas var. scribnerianum specimens lower glume is ~0.85 mm and the upper ~2.5 mm.
diagnostic_checks.compare: D. commutatum can also show purple bases but usually smaller/narrower spikelets and tiny ciliate membrane; don't force color or a single variety measurement.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: FNA species range versus UT Texas var. scribnerianum; not equivalent to exact Texas variety ID
diagnostic_checks.source: Flora of North America — Dichanthelium oligosanthes

diagnostic_review.note: Source-backed flowering phase/ligule/spikelet checklists; no same-plant spring/fall/winter photo certification or confirmed Hays County voucher.

field_rule: Look for low sprawling aboveground culms and clustered digitate one-sided racemes, then expose the INNER whitish frayed membranous ligule. Distinguish D. sanguinalis with truly paired dissected glume/lemma specimens: the labeled OTHER SPECIES plate by itself cannot verify ciliaris.
trait_provenance: Existing Hays Botany Poaceae species card morphology; preliminary multi-access character states; needs field QA

head.source: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, uploaded monocots excerpt, PDF p. 187
head.reference: Annual southern crabgrass: digitate to subdigitate racemes, versus open tumbling panicle of D. cognata.

ligule.source: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, uploaded monocots excerpt, PDF p. 186

habit.source: UT Austin PRC Digitaria ciliaris var. ciliaris; Kew GrassBase
habit.reference: Annual geniculately ascending low stems sometimes root at lower nodes or appear tufted; broad mat and tuft visual states both allowed, both photo-provisional.

diagnostic_checks.look: Count paired spikelets along the underside of each finger
diagnostic_checks.check: A typical annual southern crabgrass head has about 3–7 (sometimes more) digitate or subdigitate one-sided racemes. PAIRED spikelets sit along the angled, narrowly winged branch rachis; each spikelet has a sterile lower and fertile upper floret.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Fall witchgrass (*D. cognata*) carries mostly solitary long-stalked spikelets across a very open branched panicle, not paired units on a few fingers.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: UT Austin PRC species account; source check, attached macro photo pending
diagnostic_checks.source: UT Austin Plant Resources Center — Digitaria ciliaris

diagnostic_checks.look: Measure the tiny lower and taller upper glumes
diagnostic_checks.check: A very small triangular LOWER glume often 0.3–0.4 mm; 3-veined upper glume around 1.7–2 mm, commonly about two-thirds to three-quarters of spikelet length; lower sterile lemma generally about 7-veined and ciliate.
diagnostic_checks.compare: D. sanguinalis (comparison outside the 112-indexed set) overlaps; use glume ratio and lower-lemma vein texture, not head shape alone.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: UT Austin PRC and Kew GrassBase; photo must show both faces of same spikelet
diagnostic_checks.source: UT Austin PRC — Digitaria ciliaris spikelet anatomy

diagnostic_checks.look: Expose the membrane and follow the rooted annual base
diagnostic_checks.check: True ligule is a short membranous flap at the INNER blade–sheath junction, not hairs around a culm node. Annual culms can sprawl/root at lower nodes or rise into a loose tuft; blades may be hairy close to the throat.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Chloris fingergrass has differently arranged florets and often ciliate membranes; the grass head alone does not confirm Digitaria.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Regional UT morphological account; rooted specimen still pending
diagnostic_checks.source: UT Austin PRC — Digitaria ciliaris

diagnostic_review.note: Taxon-source anatomical prompts, not confirmed local specimen dissection or verified exact diagnostic photograph.

head.source: Peterson et al. 2014, Systematics of Disakisperma, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3817421/
head.reference: Two to fifteen subdigitate or distributed one-sided racemes; sometimes secondary hidden axillary flowers.

ligule.reference: Membranous ligule 0.5–1.5 mm, ciliate at apex; hairs at margin do not indicate hair-only ligule.

hidden_floral_heads.source: Peterson et al. 2014 Systematics of Disakisperma
hidden_floral_heads.reference: D. dubium usually makes hidden cleistogamous lateral inflorescences in lower leaf sheaths in addition to exserted terminal panicles; 4–13 florets in spikelets.

diagnostic_checks.look: Look inside the LOWEST leaf sheaths for hidden flowers
diagnostic_checks.check: In addition to exserted terminal heads, mature green sprangletop frequently produces hidden CLEISTOGAMOUS (self-pollinating, unopened) lateral spikelets inside lower leaf sheaths. These are reproductive organs, not insect galls.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Mucronate Dinebra sprangletop has a brushlike head and is not documented as routinely producing these hidden basal flowers.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Peer-reviewed genus revision, Texas vouchers; hidden structures need careful same-plant inspection
diagnostic_checks.source: Peterson et al. 2014 — Systematics of Disakisperma

diagnostic_checks.look: Count florets in one mature spikelet and measure glumes
diagnostic_checks.check: The 2014 taxonomic revision gives 4–13 florets per 4–12 mm spikelet, lower glume (1.6–)2.3–4.8 mm, upper glume 3.3–6 mm. Three-veined lemmas roughly 3.5–5 mm, typically notched or blunt.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Dinebra panicea usually has 2–4(5) florets in only 1.8–2.5 mm spikelets; counting and measurement separate similar one-sided heads.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Taxonomic revision source checked; locally measured glume/lemma photo pending
diagnostic_checks.source: Peterson et al. 2014 — Disakisperma dubium description

diagnostic_checks.look: Find a tiny membrane UNDER its hairy rim
diagnostic_checks.check: The true ligule is a 0.5–1.5 mm CILIATE MEMBRANE, sometimes visually like a fringe of hairs. Terminal panicle branches may be 2–15 and flexuous/reflexed, not necessarily strict terminal fingers.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Dinebra panicea has numerous straighter, tightly ascending rays and minute spikelets; collar hair alone cannot decide.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Published revision explicitly distinguishes membrane plus cilia; accept both broad visible states
diagnostic_checks.source: Peterson et al. 2014 — Disakisperma

awns.source: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, uploaded monocots excerpt, PDF p. 190
awns.reference: Lower lemma can be awnless or awned to over 5 cm, so preserve both broad states.

diagnostic_checks.look: Open the inner leaf collar: there is NO true ligule
diagnostic_checks.check: Barnyardgrass lacks a membranous or hair-fringe LIGULE, though the collar area can carry a few hairs. Keep 'absent' as a botanical absence, not just 'not visible in photo.'
diagnostic_checks.compare: Paspalum/Disakisperma generally have membranes and Setaria hair ligules; this is a fast high-value group character.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: FNA + Texas A&M both support absence; photo-specific collar role pending
diagnostic_checks.source: Flora of North America — Echinochloa crus-galli

diagnostic_checks.look: Compare sterile lower floret with fertile upper floret
diagnostic_checks.check: The spikelet is ~2.5–4 mm and TWO-FLORET; the LOWER sterile lemma may have no awn or a long 5 cm awn, even on the same panicle. The hardened UPPER fertile lemma has a narrower membranous tip demarcated by minute hairs (≈25× lens).
diagnostic_checks.compare: Sprangletops have several florets per spikelet, with different lemma layout; other Echinochloa species can be very similar.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: FNA anatomy supported; *E. muricata* versus *E. crus-galli* remains specimen-level
diagnostic_checks.source: Flora of North America — Echinochloa crus-galli

diagnostic_checks.look: Follow the dense branching panicle and root crown
diagnostic_checks.check: Often stout annual with 5–25 cm paniculate head; lateral branches bear dense close spikelets, sometimes with secondary branchlets. Broad awned OR awnless states must not force exclusion.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Goosegrass has relatively few flat finger branches and a short membrane, not this many-branched bristly head.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: FNA source checked; fresh local specimen and proper mature stage still needed
diagnostic_checks.source: Flora of North America — Echinochloa crus-galli

field_rule: Bob Harms's source-identified dried uprooted specimen (panel 10) shows true fibrous roots and attached flattened culms, while Harry Rose's in-situ photo (panel 1) shows field growth but hides the root crown. Goosegrass is an annual bunchgrass with notably compressed pale/whitish basal sheaths in life, NOT a network of rooting perennial runners. Neither photograph proves the LIVE milky-white crown at diagnostic close range. Next photograph: fresh uprooted living crown, fibrous roots, emerging tillers and cm scale.
trait_provenance: Existing Hays Botany Poaceae species card morphology; preliminary multi-access character states; needs field QA
broad_group: Spikes, awns, dropseeds and remaining grasses

head.source: Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas p.192
head.reference: Flattened digitate branches at culm tip, sometimes one or two inserted lower; overlapping awnless spikelets in two rows.

diagnostic_checks.look: Check the flattened whitish crown and flowering fingers
diagnostic_checks.check: Goosegrass is an ANNUAL with a conspicuously compressed, keeled, often pale-white base; a crown of 4–10(17) flat, narrow 3.5–16 cm digitate branches, sometimes with one lower branch up to 3 cm below the cluster.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Crabgrass can also have fingers but often sprawls and carries *paired two-flowered spikelets* on a winged axis.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: FNA source checked; white crown must be a live basal close-up, not an inferred color
diagnostic_checks.source: Flora of North America — Eleusine indica

diagnostic_checks.look: Count 5–7 FLORETS in a single spikelet
diagnostic_checks.check: FNA describes each 4–7 mm laterally compressed spikelet with 5–7 florets in overlapping ranks; lower glume 1.1–2.3 mm, one-veined. These are distinct from *Digitaria* two-floret spikelets.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Southern crabgrass spikelets contain sterile lower plus fertile upper floret (2 total), and Green sprangletop has 4–13 but different long branched architecture.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: FNA source checked; dissect one mature attached spikelet under 10–20×
diagnostic_checks.source: Flora of North America — Eleusine indica

diagnostic_checks.look: Locate the actual short membrane
diagnostic_checks.check: A truncate, ragged/erose membranous ligule ~0.2–1 mm occurs at the inner blade–sheath junction; nearby papillose-based throat hairs are not the ligule itself. Pale central blade vein can be a field clue.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Barnyardgrass lacks a true ligule; not all flattened weed grasses are goosegrass.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: FNA leaf-collar anatomy supported; fresh macro pending
diagnostic_checks.source: Flora of North America — Eleusine indica

field_rule: One spike with paired multiflowered spikelets establishes Elymus-type architecture; Canada vs Virginia requires mature glume feet on multiple nodes plus habit and hybrid caution. Existing Texas anatomical photographs are real, but the same-voucher measured comparison is still missing.

head.source: Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas p.192
head.reference: Typically thick nodding or oblique rye spike 8–21 cm; not sufficient alone to separate E. virginicus.

glume_base.source: Texas A&M Plants of Texas Rangelands, citing Frank Gould; FNA Elymus canadensis
glume_base.reference: Sharp V-like glume pair base and often nodding long-awned spike versus bowed U of typical Virginia wildrye; hybrids and variable erect/nodding phenotypes prevent a rigid one-criterion decision.

diagnostic_checks.look: Inspect attached glume BASES at two or more rachis nodes
diagnostic_checks.check: Canada wildrye has TWO (sometimes more) spikelets per rachis node. The pair of narrow glume bases commonly diverges sharply in a V, while Virginia wildrye's bases tend to bow into a U. View glume insertion on mature still-attached spikelets, not loose awns.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Virginia wildrye also has spikelets in pairs but more bowed, less diverging glume bases; hybrids can blur this difference.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Texas A&M comparison rooted in Gould; single-plant voucher and multiple node macros pending
diagnostic_checks.source: Texas A&M — Canada versus Virginia wildrye

diagnostic_checks.look: Follow the mature nodding or drooping SPIKE and outward-curved awns
diagnostic_checks.check: FNA allows Canada wildrye spikes about 6–30 cm, usually nodding but sometimes almost erect. Most nodes bear 2(3) spikelets, each with commonly 3–5 fertile florets and long ~15–40(50) mm outward-curving LEMMA awns; don't reject a young erect head.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Virginia wildrye spikes usually remain stiffer and erect or partly held within the flag sheath, with often shorter/straighter awns. Head direction alone is not decisive.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: FNA account, ripe and immature head photo comparison still pending
diagnostic_checks.source: Flora of North America — Elymus canadensis

diagnostic_checks.look: Identify TRUE membranous ligule and clasping auricles
diagnostic_checks.check: The inner ligule is a short ciliolate membrane usually under 1(2) mm, and 1.5–4 mm auricles can clasp the culm. These are NOT the awned glumes, which arise from the flowering spike; use the basal perennial crown too.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Virginia wildrye has falcate auricles and a short membrane; vegetative characters overlap strongly, so preserve Elymus sp. for hybrids.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: FNA; no same-specimen paired collar/glume examination yet
diagnostic_checks.source: Flora of North America — Elymus canadensis

photos.creator: Cecelia Alexander

field_rule: Open panicle alone does not separate E. intermedia from E. trichodes.
trait_provenance: Existing Hays Botany Poaceae species card morphology; preliminary multi-access character states; needs field QA

head.source: Diggs, Lipscomb & O’Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, user-provided monocots excerpt, uploaded PDF p. 194
head.reference: Flora reports an open panicle and tufted perennial form; existing airy and tuft states retained.

habit.source: UT Austin Williamson County plant account (short knotty rhizomes) vs Arizona Extension Yavapai guide (no rhizomes)
habit.reference: Some Texas source specimens described densely tufted rhizomatous base, whereas another regional account says no rhizomes. Keep broad tuft/rhizome answers eligible but do not infer rhizome from tuft photo. Verify connected belowground stem on authenticated Texas material.

diagnostic_checks.look: Check the bearded axils and where the small spikelets are borne
diagnostic_checks.check: Texas A&M describes a broadly pyramidal open panicle, with long silky hairs in the LOWERMOST branch axils; Williamson County PRC describes an even finer, widely spreading rachis and tufts of hairs on pulvini. The flowering parts are open but NOT loose terminal fingers.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Sand lovegrass can have larger oblong panicles and much longer narrow, sinuous branches; both can have hairs at branch axils.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Both regional sources support branch-axil hairs; panicle form not a stand-alone ID
diagnostic_checks.source: UT Austin Plant Resources Center — Eragrostis intermedia

diagnostic_checks.look: Dissect one mature spikelet, lemma and palea
diagnostic_checks.check: Williamson County material describes spikelets 4–7 by 1.5–1.7 mm, roughly 2–9 florets, and a 1.8–2.2 mm, three-veined lemma with inconspicuous side veins. Palea has TWO short-ciliate keels. Floret counts overlap other treatments (Texas A&M often 5–11).
diagnostic_checks.compare: Sand lovegrass has a generally larger, 2.4–3.4 mm lemma and more conspicuous terminal clusters of spikelets; use several mature spikelets.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Local UT specimen treatment and Texas A&M floret ranges differ; do not use a single exact floret count as cutoff
diagnostic_checks.source: UT Austin PRC — Eragrostis intermedia

diagnostic_checks.look: Check the fine ciliate ligule and actual underground stem
diagnostic_checks.check: UT's Williamson County specimen description gives 0.3–0.55 mm ciliate ligule with 4 mm collar hairs and mentions short knotty RHIZOMES. An Arizona field guide says non-rhizomatous. Record a connected rootstock before deciding. Pedicel/ultimate branch terminology also varies across the sources.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Purple lovegrass can have short knotty rhizomes, so shoot age and panicle dissection still matter; hair at collar does not alone identify plains lovegrass.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: REGIONAL GROWTH-CONCEPT CONFLICT; rhizome status and tiny membrane under cilia require actual field specimen
diagnostic_checks.source: UT Austin PRC — Eragrostis intermedia; contrasting Arizona Extension

diagnostic_review.note: Published source morphology; photos, local vouchers, individual organ measurements and county nativity not certified. Conflicting/variety-level traits explicitly provisional.

habit.source: Diggs, Lipscomb & O’Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, user-provided monocots excerpt, uploaded PDF p. 198
habit.reference: Flora reports tufted perennial habit; source distinguishes hairy sheath throat and sometimes villous margins. Airy head retained provisionally.

diagnostic_checks.look: Follow the long, fine spikelet pedicels through the airy panicle
diagnostic_checks.check: Kew gives an open 35–55 cm panicle, with narrow sinuous primary branches and threadlike 5–15 mm spikelet pedicels. Texas A&M describes a broad open head often 0.3–0.6 m with terminally clustered 6–10-flowered spikelets.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Plains lovegrass also has diffuse branches; use full head plus blade/sheath and exact spikelet dimensions.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Kew/GrassBase plus Texas A&M; fine stalks can be cropped out in whole-head photos
diagnostic_checks.source: Kew GrassBase — Eragrostis trichodes

diagnostic_checks.look: Compare the floral parts with plains lovegrass at the same scale
diagnostic_checks.check: Kew's typical mature spikelets are 4–10 mm, with 4–18 florets; fertile lemma about 2.4–3.4 mm, one-veined glumes. UT's local plant had ~5 mm spikelets with 4–6 florets. These ranges partly overlap E. intermedia, but lemma size and branch/pedicel architecture help.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Plains lovegrass typically has 4–7 mm spikelets and 1.8–2.2 mm lemmas in the Williamson County account. Do not exclude overlapping specimens by size alone.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Published range is broad; local voucher and multiple mature florets needed
diagnostic_checks.source: Kew GrassBase — Eragrostis trichodes

diagnostic_checks.look: Inspect both sheath THROAT hairs and the ligule
diagnostic_checks.check: Texas A&M documents a prominent tuft of hairs at the sheath throat, a short hair-fringe ligule about 0.5 mm, and a perennial rooted tuft; UT notes the collar hairs can reach about 5 mm. The long hairs near a collar are not themselves proof of a several-mm true ligule.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Plains lovegrass also has hairy throat/collar and an approximately 0.3–0.55 mm ciliate ligule; combine floral measurements.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Regional sources agree broadly; membrane base and precise hair boundary await macro photo
diagnostic_checks.source: Texas A&M Plants of Texas Rangelands — Sand Lovegrass

field_rule: Walk up from erect tuft to narrow raceme; verify actual short membranous fringed ligule; then true reproductive pattern: basal similar paired spikelets and upper unlike paired members, awned sessile fertile plus unawned pedicellate neighbor; mature long dark contorted awns and pungent brown bearded callus. Fine pair/callus requires attached scaled specimen. Photos from Australia are illustrative, not Texas occurrences.

head.source: Kew GrassBase Heteropogon contortus and Texas A&M rangeplants.tamu.edu/plant/tanglehead
head.reference: Single or few terminal racemes bearing conspicuous long dark awns that twist together into a tangled spire.

ligule.source: Smithsonian Hawaiian Flora (ciliate membrane), Kew GrassBase (hair fringe)
ligule.reference: Short ciliate membrane ~1 mm in Smithsonian; some GrassBase descriptions emphasize hair fringe. Both broad visible key states retained until actual photo shows tissue.

diagnostic_checks.look: Follow a whole raceme from base to tip
diagnostic_checks.check: Near the base the paired units are often alike, male or sterile and WITHOUT the long twisted awns; fertile sessile awned spikelets appear higher on the same raceme, beside unlike pedicelled companions.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Other bluestems with awned paired spikelets; tanglehead is not uniformly awned from bottom to top
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Smithsonian and Kew-backed; attached raceme photograph needed
diagnostic_checks.source: Smithsonian Hawaiian Flora — Heteropogon contortus

diagnostic_checks.look: Look at the sharp brown-bearded callus
diagnostic_checks.check: Mature fertile sessile spikelets are equipped with a very sharp, reddish-brown bearded callus (often 2–3 mm) and very long dark twisted awns, often about 5–12 cm; a detached unit may be prickly.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Aristida threeawns have three lemma awns; tanglehead has one long awn on each fertile sessile spikelet
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Kew/Smithsonian-backed; actual scaled callus photo pending
diagnostic_checks.source: Kew POWO / GrassBase — Heteropogon contortus

diagnostic_checks.look: Distinguish a true ligule from hairs at the collar
diagnostic_checks.check: Smithsonian describes a short CILIATE MEMBRANE about 1 mm; other GrassBase treatments call it a hair fringe. Keep both broad visual states provisionally and inspect the tissue in a real collar macro.
diagnostic_checks.compare: The ligule alone does not separate tanglehead from other Andropogoneae
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Cross-source terminology variation, photo check pending
diagnostic_checks.source: Smithsonian Hawaiian Flora — Heteropogon contortus

field_rule: Genus: 3 ONE-FLOWERED spikelets on one barley rachis node. Species: little annual narrow erect spike + short straight glumes; foxtail = nodding feather with longer splayed glumes and perennial base. Detached awned group is NOT confirmation of the central fertile spikelet; get attached node macro.
trait_provenance: Existing Hays Botany Poaceae species card morphology; preliminary multi-access character states; needs field QA
broad_group: Spikes, awns, dropseeds and remaining grasses

head.source: Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas p.202
head.reference: Small erect flattened barley spike; at nodes, three one-flowered spikelets; bristled spike is not a foxtail of sterile-branch bristles.

diagnostic_checks.look: Count THREE ONE-FLORET spikelets at each rachis node
diagnostic_checks.check: Little barley has a CENTRAL normally fertile spikelet with two LATERAL spikelets, usually reduced/sterile, all grouped at one rachis node. Awn-like glumes surround the node; don't mistake the three spikelets for three lemma awns on one floret.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Cereal rye generally has ONE spikelet per spike node, typically with 2(3) florets; Elymus generally has paired MULTIFLORET spikelets.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: FNA and UT Williamson County anatomy; magnified attached triplet/photo pending
diagnostic_checks.source: Flora of North America — Hordeum pusillum

diagnostic_checks.look: Inspect the annual crown, little erect barley head and ligule
diagnostic_checks.check: A small usually annual and non-rosetted tuft with an erect, sometimes flag-sheath-embraced 2–9 cm head. True ligule is a 0.2–0.8 mm MEMBRANE, not a beard of awns. Winter green annual basal leaves may exist before spring heads.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Foxtail barley species are often larger/perennial and carry more divergent, feathery glume awns; little barley glumes usually straight or little divergent.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: FNA and regional Williamson County source; real winter stage/connected root still photo pending
diagnostic_checks.source: UT Austin — Hordeum pusillum

diagnostic_checks.look: Separate central from reduced lateral FLORETS
diagnostic_checks.check: FNA central spikelet glumes are flattened at the base, and its lemma is about 5–8.5 mm with often 3.5–9.5 mm awn. Lateral spikelets have reduced florets, frequently shorter than the central. Count florets INSIDE each member of triplet, not at the entire node.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Cereal rye has generally two functional florets in one spikelet; cultivated barley can bear seed in all three spikelets of a node and must not be assumed H. pusillum.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Published ranges and lateral reduction vary; same-mature-node dissection pending
diagnostic_checks.source: Flora of North America — Hordeum pusillum
